blocks.text: Taste is sensed by special chemoreceptors, the taste buds. There are about 10,000, mostly between bumps called papillae on the tongue, with some in the throat and on the roof of the mouth. A taste bud is bulb-shaped, made of receptor cells with hair-like tips and basal cells that make new receptor cells, and opens into the mouth through a taste pore.

When chemicals in food or drink stimulate the receptor cells, they produce impulses in sensory neurons, which travel along cranial nerves VII, IX and X to the brainstem and then to the taste areas of the cerebral cortex. The cortex combines this with other information, such as smell and texture, into the full perception of taste.

The book describes four kinds of taste bud, for salty, sweet, sour and bitter, concentrated in regions of the tongue: sweet at the tip, sour at the sides, bitter at the back and salty over most of the surface, with overlaps.

blocks.alt: Left: a bulb-shaped taste bud set in the surface of the tongue, with long receptor cells whose hair-like tips reach a taste pore, basal cells at the base and sensory nerve fibres below. Right: the olfactory bulb above a plate of bone; olfactory neurons pass down through the bone between grey supporting cells, and their cilia lie in a layer of mucus where odour molecules from the air dissolve.

blocks.long_description: Taste buds (about 10,000) are chemoreceptors, mostly between the papillae of the tongue; each opens through a taste pore and has receptor cells and basal cells that replace them. Chemicals in food stimulate the receptor cells, and impulses travel along cranial nerves VII, IX and X to the brainstem and then the taste areas of the cerebral cortex. Smell receptors are the ends of sensory neurons in the nasal epithelium, between supporting cells and basal cells; odour chemicals dissolve in the mucus, bind to the cilia, and impulses pass along the olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) to the olfactory bulb.

blocks.title: Note on the text
blocks.text: The 'tongue map' of taste regions is now regarded as outdated: taste buds all over the tongue respond to every basic taste, with small differences in sensitivity. Most textbooks also add a fifth basic taste, umami (savoury).

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Smell affects taste: eat a piece of onion with your nose open, then with your nose plugged, and compare.

blocks.prompt: Which cranial nerves carry taste impulses to the brainstem?
blocks.explanation: Cranial nerves VII, IX and X.

items: About 10,000 taste buds (receptor cells, basal cells, taste pore); impulses via nerves VII, IX, X to the brainstem and cortex; smell adds to taste.
